insider_note: Checking that the integrand is even is worth doing on any symmetric-limits integral (−a to a) before starting — if it were odd, the answer would just be 0 with no further work needed.

steps.label: Show the integrand is even
steps.margin_note: One mark. f(−x) = f(x) must be checked, not assumed.
steps.memory_tip: A function built only from x² and even powers of x is always even — check f(−x) = f(x) to confirm.
lines: The limits are −a and a, so first check

lines.text: whether the integrand is even or odd.

steps.why: Both x² and (a² − x²) depend only on x², so replacing x by −x leaves the expression unchanged — the definition of an even function.
common_mistakes: Assuming the function is even without writing out the f(−x) check.

steps.label: Reduce to twice the 0-to-a integral
steps.margin_note: One more mark. This is a standard rule for even functions on symmetric limits.
steps.memory_tip: ∫₋ₐᵃ (even function) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ (same function) dx — always halves the work for an even integrand.
steps.why: An even function's graph is a mirror image about the y-axis, so the area from −a to 0 exactly equals the area from 0 to a — the whole integral is twice the half-interval integral.
common_mistakes: Applying this rule to a function that has not actually been shown to be even.

steps.label: Substitute x = a sinθ
steps.margin_note: One mark. The same standard substitution as any (a²−x²) power.
steps.memory_tip: x = a sinθ turns a² − x² into a²cos²θ, a perfect square, whenever a power of (a²−x²) appears.
lines: Put x = a sinθ ⇒ dx = a cosθ dθ. x = 0

lines.text: Then a² − x² = a²cos²θ, whose root is a cosθ,

steps.why: x = a sinθ makes a² − x² = a²cos²θ, whose 3/2 power is a³cos³θ; combining the extra a cosθ from dx collects every constant factor into a single a⁶ outside the integral.
common_mistakes: Missing one of the powers of a when combining a²·a³·a = a⁶.
Writing (√(a²cos²θ))³ as a³cos²θ instead of the correct a³cos³θ.
lines_compact: Put x = a sinθ ⇒ dx = a cosθ dθ. x = 0

steps.label: Apply Wallis's formula
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Both powers in sin²θcos⁴θ are even (2 and 4), so Wallis's formula carries the extra π/2 factor.
steps.memory_tip: ∫ sin²θcos⁴θ dθ from 0 to π/2 is (1)(3·1)/(6·4·2) · π/2 — both powers 2 and 4 are even, so the extra π/2 factor is included.

lines.text: Wallis's formula for sinᵐθ cosⁿθ, m = 2, n = 4:

steps.why: With both powers (2 and 4) even, Wallis's formula includes the extra π/2 factor; multiplying by the outer 2a⁶ and simplifying the fraction gives the final closed form.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the extra π/2 factor since both powers are even.
An arithmetic slip in reducing 2a⁶·π/32 to πa⁶/16.
